THOUGHT: Young male with significant mucosal bleeding after dental extraction and a lifetime history of easy bruising, plus a male relative (uncle) with similar bleeding and joint swelling — pattern suggests an X‑linked congenital bleeding disorder. Laboratory evaluation shows an isolated prolonged PTT (60 s) with normal-to-near-normal PT, normal platelet count and bleeding time, normal peripheral smear, and no evidence of fibrinolysis/DIC. This pattern localizes to the intrinsic coagulation pathway (factor VIII or IX deficiency). von Willebrand disease and platelet disorders are unlikely because bleeding time is normal and platelets are normal. Acquired inhibitors (eg, lupus anticoagulant) typically do not present with bleeding, and liver disease/DIC are not supported. Between intrinsic factor deficiencies, hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) is far more common than hemophilia B. The family history of joint swelling (hemarthroses) also fits hemophilia. Therefore the most likely diagnosis is hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency).

DIAGNOSIS: Hemophilia A (congenital factor VIII deficiency)
